coverageNotes: Tests native compound-index ordering and bounded selection. Does not measure production performance, schema design, or independent implementation. Tied priorities are allowed.

questions.concept: Compound equality leaves the next field ordered
questions.context:
Using Convex 1.44.0, tasks has fields projectId: string, status: string, priority: number, title: string, assignee: string and .index("by_project_status_priority", ["projectId", "status", "priority"]). Seven tasks for projectId="p" and status="todo" were inserted in this order: priorities [9, 2, 7, 1, 5, 3, 4]. Other projects and statuses also exist. A query validates projectId and status as strings and runs:

```ts
return await ctx.db.query("tasks")
  .withIndex("by_project_status_priority", (q) =>
    q.eq("projectId", args.projectId).eq("status", args.status))
  .take(5);
```
questions.question: For { projectId: "p", status: "todo" }, which priority sequence does the query return?

options.text: [9, 2, 7, 1, 5], following creation order within the equality range.
options.rationale: Creation order is not the next ordering field here. A table-scan control follows creation order; the displayed compound index follows priority.

options.text: [9, 7, 5, 4, 3], following descending priority within the equality range.
options.rationale: Descending priority requires order("desc"); that targeted control returns this sequence.

options.text: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], following ascending priority within the equality range.
options.rationale: After fixing projectId and status, priority is the next index field. The default ascending traversal and take(5) return the five smallest priorities.

options.text: It throws because priority must also have an equality constraint before take(5).
options.rationale: A compound-index query may constrain just its leading equality prefix. The exact query typechecks, deploys and runs without constraining priority.
